intent: Draw an explicit boundary inside which one model of the domain is defined and valid, so each part of a large system can be modelled rigorously without a single compromised global model.
problem: A single model spanning a complex domain accumulates incompatible interpretations of the same terms until every change is a negotiation, every concept is polysemous, and the result is the big ball of mud: a model nobody can hold and everybody shares.
context: A bounded context is a description of a boundary — typically a subsystem or a team's work — within which a particular model is defined and applicable. Context determines the meaning of a statement: the same word can mean different things, legitimately, in different contexts. The decisive boundary is usually human (a team, a language, a product line) rather than technical, because the model acts as the Ubiquitous Language and you need a different model when the language changes. Evans is explicit that bounded contexts and subdomains do not coincide: reorganising around subdomains can leave the contexts misaligned, and two teams sharing one context is a reliable route to mud.
benefits: Each model can be internally consistent, because consistency is only required inside the boundary.
Polysemous concepts are legitimate across contexts instead of being averaged into a mush.
Teams can evolve models independently; a change in one context does not force changes in the others.
The ubiquitous language becomes enforceable — there is a defined place where a term has one meaning.
New functionality can be grafted into a legacy system by defining a new context rather than rewriting the old one.
tradeoffs: Translation between contexts is now a real cost, paid in an anti-corruption layer, a translation layer or by conforming.
The boundary must be enforced continuously (continuous integration inside the context); a context that is not kept sound becomes mud.
Splitting one bounded context into several can be more expensive than the model inconsistency it fixes.
Business data may need duplication across contexts, with a reconciliation process.
A single-team monolith gains little: the overhead is only justified when the domain genuinely splits.
quality_attributes_note: simplicity 5 because boundaries and translation cost money. scalability 8 because independent contexts deploy and scale independently.

participants.responsibility: The boundary within which one model is defined and applicable.
participants.notes: It is a description of a boundary, not necessarily a deployable unit.

participants.responsibility: The system of abstractions that is valid only inside the boundary.
participants.notes: Statements about a model can only be understood in a context.

participants.responsibility: The shared language that makes the model coherent within the boundary.
participants.notes: Once a bounded context is defined, we must keep it sound.

participants.responsibility: The explicit drawing of how contexts relate, and which relationship pattern governs each edge.
participants.notes: Evans: several services designed to work with each other together form a bounded context.

use_cases: Splitting a monolith where "Customer" means account holder in one module and billing contact in another.
Defining a new context around new functionality grafted onto a legacy system instead of rewriting it.
Making the boundary between an in-memory model and a relational model explicit rather than implicit.
Giving a subcontractor a narrow context with its own model so the core domain is not diluted.
Drawing the boundary between an interchange context (all messages and schemas, no services) and the service contexts around it.
avoid_when: The domain is simple enough that one model is rigorous — the overhead buys nothing.
Two contexts would contain the same model and the same language; that is one context with two code bases.
The boundary has no team, no language and no different model behind it — it is a package, not a context.
You are drawing it to justify a microservice split rather than a model boundary.
pitfalls: Confusing bounded context with subdomain; they often but not always coincide, and the misalignment is a real trap.
Letting two teams work in the same bounded context, which reliably produces a big ball of mud.
Fixing the boundary at the technical layer while the language still spans both sides.
Sharing a database schema between contexts so the models drift silently despite the boundary.
Naming contexts after organisational units instead of after the model they contain.

related_patterns_notes.context-mapping: A bounded context is a node on the context map; context-mapping is how you decide what kind of edge leaves it.
related_patterns_notes.ubiquitous-language: The bounded context is the scope in which a ubiquitous language has exactly one meaning per term.
related_patterns_notes.anti-corruption-layer: The translation mechanism that lets one context keep its model intact against another's.
related_patterns_notes.domain-model: Bounded Context bounds the model; the domain model is what lives inside it.

anti_patterns: One global entity model shared by every bounded context.
A "context" that is only a deployable unit with no distinct model or language behind it.
A boundary drawn at the database, so the model still leaks across it.
Contexts that overlap, so a single change requires editing two of them.
Treating the context map as a one-off diagram that is never revisited as the system evolves.
design_principles: Explicitly define the context within which a model applies, and set boundaries in terms of team organisation, usage and physical manifestation (code bases, schemas).
Keep the model strictly consistent within the bounds and do not be distracted by issues outside.
Once a bounded context has been defined, we must keep it sound — institute continuous integration and exercise the ubiquitous language.
DDD divides a large system into bounded contexts, each of which can have a unified model.
Speak a ubiquitous language within an explicitly bounded context.
best_practices: Name the context after the model it contains, and document what the boundary deliberately excludes.
Draw the context map early, and re-draw it whenever a new integration appears.
Keep a shared database out of a boundary; a context that reads another context's tables has no boundary.
Use an anti-corruption layer at every edge where the downstream model must not be contaminated.
Test at the context boundaries — the integration is where the bugs live.
Distinguish the service contexts from the interchange context, which owns only messages, schemas and protocols.
